newsitem.title: ROMANIA: ROMANIA PRESIDENT PRESSES PRIVATISATION RESHUFFLE.
newsitem.headline: ROMANIA PRESIDENT PRESSES PRIVATISATION RESHUFFLE.

text.p: Reformist President Emil Constantinescu named five members to the board of Romania's top privatisation agency on Monday, nearly completing a shake-up denounced by his leftist opponents as "political cleansing".

The board of the State Ownership Fund, appointed by the president, parliament and government, has been all but cleared of members of the leftist Party of Social Democracy (PDSR), ousted in November's general and presidential elections.

Constantinescu's appointees included one member of the National Peasant Party, the backbone of the centrist coalition which took power after the election. The president's press office said the others had no political affiliation.
The government is committed to speeding up privatisation and other market reforms which ministers say were stalled under its leftist predecessor.
An International Monetary Fund team is holding talks with ministers to work out the details of a reform programme and restore the Fund's credits suspended last year.
Appointments to the Fund's board in the past three days by the government and the lower house of parliament ousted several PDSR members in favour of members of the ruling coalition.
Former Foreign Minister Teodor Melescanu, now a PDSR spokesman, vowed to complain to the Council of Europe.

"We view what is going on now as political cleansing and we intend to complain to the Council of Europe," Melescanu told state television before leaving for the Council's parliamentary winter session in the French city of Strasbourg.

But leading politicians within the coalition say the changes are necessary to proceed with change. Four members must still be appointed to the 17-strong board -- one from the government and three from parliament's upper house.

The Fund has been accused of stalling the selloff of equity in some 6,500 companies in its administration. It has been put under scrutiny over alleged irregulaties by undervaluing the capital of some of the 3,000 companies it has turned private.
